title: AP World History
description: Free AP World History study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: The Global Tapestry 1200-1450

concepts.intro: By 1200, the Islamic world stretched from Iberia to Southeast Asia, unified by trade, faith, and Arabic scholarship even as political power fragmented after the Abbasid Caliphate's decline.
b: Abbasid Caliphate (750-1258) centered in Baghdad, a hub of science, math, and Greek text preservation until the 1258 Mongol sack
Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) brought Islamic rule to South Asia, taxing (jizya) non-Muslims and blending Persian-Islamic and Hindu culture
Sufism (mystical Islam) and traveling scholars like Ibn Battuta spread Islamic practice into West Africa and Southeast Asia
Mansa Musa's Mali (r. 1312-1337) tied West Africa into the Dar al-Islam via his famous 1324 hajj through Cairo
Cordoba in Islamic Spain (al-Andalus) was a center of learning where Muslim, Jewish, and Christian scholars translated classical texts

concepts.l: China: Song, Yuan, and Ming Dynasties
concepts.intro: China led the world in technology, bureaucracy, and trade, alternating between periods of dynastic strength and Mongol conquest.
b: Song Dynasty (960-1279) had the civil service exam based on Confucian classics, movable type printing, and gunpowder weapons
Champa rice from Vietnam, adopted under the Song, allowed double-cropping and fueled population growth
Yuan Dynasty (1271-1368) was founded by Kublai Khan after the Mongol conquest of China, using foreigners (like Marco Polo) in administration
Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) overthrew Mongol rule and restored Confucian bureaucracy and the civil service exam
Zheng He's treasure fleet voyages (1405-1433) under the Ming projected Chinese power across the Indian Ocean before China turned inward

concepts.intro: West and East African states built wealth through trans-Saharan gold-salt trade and Indian Ocean commerce, developing distinct political and religious systems.
b: Mali Empire controlled trans-Saharan trade routes, taxing gold and salt exchanged at Timbuktu and Gao
Great Zimbabwe (c. 1100-1450) was a stone-built trading state linked to Indian Ocean gold and ivory trade with Swahili coast cities
Swahili Coast city-states (Kilwa, Mombasa, Mogadishu) blended Bantu and Islamic culture, speaking Swahili and trading gold, ivory, and slaves for Indian Ocean goods
Axum/Ethiopia remained a Christian kingdom, isolated but resilient amid surrounding Islamic states
Griots (oral historians) preserved West African political and cultural history absent widespread written records

concepts.intro: Medieval Europe was politically fragmented under feudalism while the Byzantine Empire preserved Roman-Christian tradition in the east until its final decline.
b: Feudalism organized medieval Europe: land-for-loyalty relationships between lords, vassals, and serfs
The Catholic Church was the unifying institution of Western Europe, controlling education and legitimizing monarchs
The Byzantine Empire (capital Constantinople) preserved Greco-Roman learning and Orthodox Christianity, acting as a buffer against Islamic expansion
The Great Schism (1054) formally split Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Christianity
The Crusades (1095-1291) were religious wars for the Holy Land that increased European contact with Islamic and Byzantine goods and ideas

concepts.intro: In the Western Hemisphere, isolated from Afro-Eurasian networks, the Mexica and Inca built large tribute-based empires through conquest and engineering.
b: The Mexica (Aztec) Empire, capital Tenochtitlan (founded 1325), ruled central Mexico through a tribute system extracted from conquered peoples
Aztec religion demanded human sacrifice to sustain the sun god Huitzilopochtli, justifying wars to capture victims
The Inca Empire ran along the Andes with the capital at Cuzco, using the mit'a labor tax system instead of currency
Inca administration used quipu (knotted cords) for record-keeping and an extensive road system for control without writing
Both empires lacked large draft animals, wheeled transport, and steel, unlike contemporary Afro-Eurasian states

concepts.intro: States across the globe 1200-1450 used comparable strategies—bureaucracy, religion, military, and tribute—to organize diverse populations and legitimize rule.
b: Bureaucracies (Chinese civil service, Islamic caliphate administration) recruited talent and enforced central control
Religion legitimized rulers everywhere: Mandate of Heaven in China, divine right of Islamic caliphs, Aztec sun worship
Military conquest and tribute/tax systems (Mongol tribute, Aztec tribute, mit'a) extracted resources from subject peoples
Trade networks (Silk Roads, Indian Ocean, trans-Saharan) linked empires and spread technology, religion, and disease before 1450
Comparison is key on the AP exam: know similarities/differences in how states justified and maintained power

keyFacts: The Mongols had not yet unified Eurasia in this period's earliest years, but by mid-1200s the Mongol Empire was the largest contiguous land empire in history.
Mansa Musa's hajj (1324-1325) spent so much gold in Cairo it reportedly depressed the region's gold value for years.
Zheng He's voyages preceded European Age of Exploration by nearly a century but were discontinued when the Ming turned to isolationism.
The Aztec and Inca empires developed complex administrative systems without the wheel, iron tools, or a fully alphabetic writing system.
traps: The Crusades were primarily religious/military campaigns for Jerusalem, not simple 'trade expeditions' — though they did increase European exposure to Asian goods.
The Delhi Sultanate ruled over a Hindu-majority population; it did not convert all of South Asia to Islam, and Hindu-Muslim syncretism (e.g., Sikhism later) emerged from this contact.
Feudalism in Europe was decentralized power-sharing, not a strong centralized monarchy like Song China or the Mali Empire.
The Inca used the mit'a labor/tax system, not currency-based taxation — don't confuse it with European feudal dues.

units.name: Networks of Exchange

concepts.intro: Overland trade routes connecting East Asia to the Mediterranean carried goods, technology, religions, and disease across Eurasia, reaching a peak under the Mongol-enforced Pax Mongolica.
b: Connected China, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe, exchanging silk, spices, paper, and gunpowder technology
Buddhism spread from India into China and Central Asia via Silk Road merchants and monks
Caravanserais (roadside inns) supported long-distance overland merchants across arid Central Asian terrain
The Pax Mongolica (13th-14th century) secured Silk Road routes under unified Mongol control, boosting trade volume and safety
The Black Death (bubonic plague) traveled along the Silk Roads from Central Asia into Europe and the Middle East in the 1340s

concepts.intro: Monsoon winds enabled a vast maritime trading system linking East Africa, Arabia, India, Southeast Asia, and China in the era's largest and most lucrative trade network.
b: Predictable monsoon wind patterns allowed merchants to sail reliably between regions in different seasons
Key port cities included Calicut and Malacca (Melaka), major transshipment hubs for spices and goods
Dhows (Arab/Indian ships) and Chinese junks were the dominant vessels, larger and more advanced than most contemporary European ships
Goods traded included spices (pepper, cloves), textiles (Indian cotton), porcelain, and gold
Swahili Coast cities and Gujarati merchants were key intermediaries connecting African, Middle Eastern, and Asian markets

concepts.intro: Camel caravans crossed the Sahara Desert linking West African gold and salt producers to North African and Mediterranean markets, spreading Islam southward.
b: Gold from West Africa (Mali, Ghana, Songhai) was exchanged for salt mined in the Sahara at cities like Taghaza
The camel saddle and caravan organization made regular desert crossings possible starting centuries earlier and intensifying in this era
Timbuktu and Gao grew into wealthy trade and Islamic scholarly centers due to their position on these routes
Islam spread into West Africa largely through Muslim merchants engaged in trans-Saharan trade, not military conquest
The Mali Empire taxed trade passing through its territory, becoming enormously wealthy, as shown by Mansa Musa's hajj

concepts.l: The Mongol Empire and Its Effects
concepts.intro: The Mongols under Chinggis (Genghis) Khan built history's largest contiguous land empire, which unified Eurasian trade routes despite immense destruction during conquest.
b: Chinggis Khan united Mongol tribes and began conquests that eventually stretched from China to Eastern Europe
The empire split into four khanates: the Yuan (China), Golden Horde (Russia), Ilkhanate (Persia/Middle East), and Chagatai Khanate (Central Asia)
Mongol rule enforced relative safety and stability along the Silk Roads (Pax Mongolica), facilitating merchant travel like Marco Polo's
Mongols were generally religiously tolerant, adopting elements of the cultures they conquered (e.g., Yuan rulers adopted some Chinese customs)
The Mongols also facilitated the spread of the bubonic plague along trade routes, contributing to demographic collapse in Eurasia

concepts.intro: Trade networks spread transformative technologies—papermaking, printing, gunpowder, and navigation tools—that reshaped societies far from their point of origin.
b: Papermaking technology spread from China westward through the Islamic world and eventually to Europe
Gunpowder, invented in China, spread via trade and Mongol conquests, eventually revolutionizing warfare in the Islamic world and Europe
The magnetic compass, developed in China, improved maritime navigation, aiding Indian Ocean and later Atlantic voyages
Astrolabes, refined by Islamic scholars building on Greek models, helped sailors determine latitude at sea
Printing technology (woodblock, then movable type) spread from China, influencing later developments including the Gutenberg press in Europe

concepts.intro: Expanded trade networks were double-edged: they spread religions and ideas that reshaped societies, but also carried the Black Death, which devastated populations across Afro-Eurasia.
b: The Black Death (1340s-1350s) killed an estimated one-third of Europe's population and caused similar devastation in the Middle East and China
Labor shortages after the plague weakened the manorial/feudal system in Europe, raising the bargaining power of surviving peasants
Buddhism, Islam, and Christianity all spread significantly via trade networks and merchant/missionary activity in this period
Cultural diffusion via trade also spread artistic styles, culinary crops, and scientific knowledge (e.g., Hindu-Arabic numerals) across regions
Trade networks fostered diaspora communities, such as Muslim merchant communities settling in Indian Ocean port cities

keyFacts: The three great trade networks of this era were the Silk Roads (overland), the Indian Ocean network (maritime, monsoon-driven), and the trans-Saharan routes (desert caravan).
The Mongol Empire's unification of Eurasian trade routes (Pax Mongolica) is a prime example of how political stability boosted long-distance commerce.
The Black Death, spread via Silk Road and Mongol trade contacts, killed roughly a third of Europe's population and caused major social and economic change.
Religions (Buddhism, Islam) spread primarily through peaceful means — merchants, missionaries, and Sufi mystics — along these trade networks, not solely through conquest.
traps: The Indian Ocean trade network relied on monsoon winds, not constant winds like the Atlantic — sailing seasons were dictated by wind direction reversal.
Islam spread into West Africa mainly through trans-Saharan trade contact and voluntary conversion by elites, not primarily through military jihad.
The Mongols did not destroy all trade — while conquest was brutal, the resulting empire's stability (Pax Mongolica) actually increased Silk Road trade volume.
The Black Death originated in Central Asia and spread via trade routes; it was not a European-only phenomenon — it also devastated the Middle East and China.

units.name: Land-Based Empires

concepts.intro: The Ottoman Turks built a powerful Islamic empire spanning three continents, famously capturing Constantinople in 1453 and ruling a diverse population through the millet system.
b: Mehmed II ('the Conqueror') captured Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire and renaming the city Istanbul
The Ottomans used gunpowder cannons effectively to breach Constantinople's walls, showcasing the era's 'gunpowder empire' military edge
The millet system allowed religious minorities (Christians, Jews) to govern their own communities under Ottoman rule, paying a jizya tax
The devshirme system conscripted Christian boys from the Balkans, converting and training them as elite Janissary soldiers or administrators
Suleiman the Magnificent (r. 1520-1566) presided over the empire's peak, expanding into the Balkans and reforming law

concepts.intro: The Safavid Empire made Twelver Shia Islam the official state religion of Persia, creating a lasting Sunni-Shia divide with its Ottoman rivals.
b: Founded by Ismail I in 1501, the Safavids forcibly converted Persia to Shia Islam, distinguishing it from Sunni neighbors
The Ottoman-Safavid rivalry was partly religious (Sunni vs. Shia) and partly a struggle for control of trade routes and territory
Shah Abbas I (r. 1588-1629) reached the empire's height, reforming the military and promoting trade at the capital Isfahan
Isfahan became a dazzling center of Persian art, architecture, and carpet-weaving under Safavid patronage
The Safavids used gunpowder weapons and a professional standing army to consolidate central power, another 'gunpowder empire'

concepts.intro: The Mughal Empire united most of South Asia under Muslim rule, blending Persian, Islamic, and Hindu traditions and reaching a cultural and administrative peak under Akbar.
b: Founded by Babur in 1526 after the Battle of Panipat, the Mughal Empire ruled most of the Indian subcontinent
Akbar the Great (r. 1556-1605) promoted religious tolerance, abolishing the jizya tax on Hindus and marrying into Hindu Rajput families
Akbar created a policy of Sulh-i-kul ('universal peace/tolerance') blending Hindu and Muslim administrative elites
Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal (completed 1653) as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, showcasing Mughal architectural grandeur
Aurangzeb (r. 1658-1707) reversed tolerant policies, reinstating the jizya and enforcing stricter Islamic law, straining Hindu-Muslim relations

concepts.intro: China alternated between the ethnically Chinese Ming Dynasty and the Manchu-led Qing Dynasty, both maintaining centralized bureaucratic rule and periods of relative isolation from the West.
b: The Ming Dynasty (1368-1644) restored Confucian bureaucracy and briefly projected naval power via Zheng He before turning inward
The Ming built and restored the Great Wall of China as defense against northern nomadic incursions (notably the Mongols)
The Qing Dynasty (1644-1912) was founded by the Manchus, who conquered Ming China while maintaining the civil service examination system
Kangxi and Qianlong emperors expanded Qing territory significantly, doubling China's size and stabilizing long-term rule
Both dynasties limited European trade contact, restricting foreign merchants largely to controlled ports like Canton (Guangzhou) under the Qing

concepts.intro: Moscow's grand princes threw off Mongol ('Tatar') control and built a centralized, autocratic Russian state that expanded eastward across Siberia.
b: Ivan III ('the Great') ended Mongol/Tatar dominance over Moscow in 1480, asserting Russian independence
Ivan IV ('the Terrible') became the first to take the title Tsar (Caesar), centralizing power and expanding Russian territory
The Russian Orthodox Church legitimized tsarist rule, with Moscow proclaimed the 'Third Rome' after Constantinople's fall
Serfdom bound Russian peasants to the land, becoming a defining and long-lasting feature of the Russian social/economic system
Peter the Great (r. 1682-1725) later westernized Russia's military, bureaucracy, and culture, founding St. Petersburg as a 'window to the West'

concepts.intro: Historians group the Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal, Ming/Qing, and Russian states as 'gunpowder empires' whose rulers used firearms and cannon to centralize power over vast land territories.
b: All these empires used gunpowder weaponry to defeat rivals and consolidate centralized, absolutist rule over diverse populations
Religious legitimacy (Sunni Islam, Shia Islam, Confucianism, Orthodox Christianity) underpinned each ruler's claim to authority
Bureaucracies (Ottoman devshirme-trained officials, Chinese scholar-officials, Mughal mansabdars) administered these vast territories
Religious diversity management varied: Ottomans and Mughals under Akbar tolerated minorities, while Safavids and later Aurangzeb enforced religious conformity
Trade and taxation of agricultural land (not maritime commerce alone) were the primary revenue sources for these land-based empires

keyFacts: The 'gunpowder empires' — Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal — used cannon and firearms to centralize power over large land empires between roughly 1450-1750.
The Ottoman capture of Constantinople in 1453 ended the Byzantine Empire and marked a major shift in Mediterranean and European power.
Religious tolerance policy varied dramatically by ruler: Akbar's tolerance contrasts sharply with Aurangzeb's later enforcement of Islamic orthodoxy in Mughal India.
The Qing Dynasty, founded by the non-Chinese Manchus, nonetheless preserved the Confucian civil service exam system to legitimize and staff its bureaucracy.
traps: The Ottoman millet system granted religious communities self-governance, not equal political power — it was tolerance for social order, not democracy.
The Safavid-Ottoman rivalry was about Shia vs. Sunni Islam and territorial control, not a simple 'Christian vs. Muslim' conflict.
Akbar's religious tolerance was a personal policy, not a permanent Mughal norm — Aurangzeb later reversed many of these tolerant practices.
Russia's tsarist system developed by rejecting Mongol overlordship, not by adopting Mongol governance structures — 'Third Rome' ideology ties Russia to Byzantine Orthodoxy, not the Mongols.

units.name: Transoceanic Connections 1450-1750

concepts.intro: Portugal and Spain pioneered transoceanic voyages driven by the search for direct routes to Asian spices, Christian missionary zeal, and new navigational technology.
b: Prince Henry the Navigator sponsored Portuguese voyages down the West African coast starting in the 1420s, seeking a sea route to Asia
Vasco da Gama reached India by sailing around Africa in 1498, opening a direct sea route to Indian Ocean spice markets
Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean in 1492 seeking a westward route to Asia, initiating sustained contact with the Americas
The caravel ship design, combining European and Islamic/Chinese navigational features, enabled longer ocean voyages against the wind
Motives for exploration are often summarized as 'God, Gold, and Glory' — religious conversion, economic profit, and national/personal prestige

concepts.intro: Contact between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres after 1492 triggered a massive global transfer of crops, animals, people, and diseases with transformative and often devastating effects.
b: New World crops (maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao) transformed diets and supported population growth in Afro-Eurasia
Old World crops and animals (wheat, sugar, horses, cattle, pigs) were introduced to the Americas, reshaping agriculture and Indigenous life
Old World diseases (smallpox, measles, influenza) devastated Indigenous American populations, which lacked immunity, killing an estimated 80-90% in some regions
The horse, reintroduced to the Americas, transformed the mobility and warfare of Plains Indigenous peoples
Silver from Spanish American mines (Potosí) entered global trade circuits, notably fueling trade with Ming/Qing China via the Manila Galleon

concepts.intro: Spain and Portugal established the first major European colonial empires in the Americas, extracting resources through forced labor systems and imposing Catholicism on Indigenous populations.
b: Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec Empire (1519-1521) with the aid of Indigenous allies, disease, and superior weaponry
Francisco Pizarro conquered the Inca Empire (1532-1533), exploiting a civil war and capturing the emperor Atahualpa
The encomienda system granted Spanish colonists the right to Indigenous labor and tribute in exchange for 'protection' and conversion
The mita system was adapted by Spain from Inca labor practices to force Indigenous workers into silver mines like Potosí under brutal conditions
Portuguese colonization focused more on coastal trading posts and Brazil, developing large sugar plantations reliant on enslaved labor

concepts.intro: As Indigenous populations collapsed from disease and overwork, European colonizers turned to the forced transportation of enslaved Africans to the Americas, creating a brutal, large-scale system of racialized slavery.
b: An estimated 12+ million enslaved Africans were forcibly transported to the Americas between the 16th and 19th centuries
The Middle Passage refers to the horrific transatlantic voyage; mortality rates were extremely high due to disease, abuse, and overcrowding
The triangular trade linked Europe (manufactured goods), West Africa (enslaved people), and the Americas (raw materials like sugar and tobacco)
African states and merchants (such as the Kingdom of Kongo, Dahomey, and Asante) participated in supplying captives, often obtained through warfare
Racial hierarchies and chattel slavery ideology developed to justify the permanent, hereditary enslavement of Africans specifically

concepts.intro: Colonizing powers developed varied coerced labor systems—encomienda, mita, chattel slavery, and indentured servitude—to extract wealth from American colonies.
b: Chattel slavery treated enslaved Africans and their descendants as permanent, inheritable property, distinct from earlier forms of bondage
Cash crop plantation agriculture (sugar in Brazil/Caribbean, tobacco in Virginia) relied heavily on enslaved labor for profitability
Silver mining in Spanish America (Potosí, Zacatecas) used forced Indigenous (mita) and later some enslaved labor under brutal conditions
Indentured servitude bound mostly poorer Europeans to a fixed term of labor in exchange for passage to the colonies
These labor systems created deeply hierarchical, race-based colonial societies (e.g., the casta system in Spanish America)

concepts.intro: European monarchs used the wealth and administrative demands of overseas empire to strengthen centralized, often absolutist state power at home.
b: Absolutism concentrated political power in monarchs like Louis XIV of France, who claimed divine right and reduced noble political influence
Mercantilism, the dominant economic theory, held that colonies existed to enrich the mother country through favorable trade balances and raw material extraction
Joint-stock companies (Dutch and British East India Companies) pooled investor capital to fund risky, profitable overseas trading ventures
Growing maritime empires funded standing armies and navies, reinforcing monarchical power and enabling further imperial competition
Religious wars (e.g., following the Protestant Reformation) intertwined with state consolidation as rulers used religion to unify or control territory

keyFacts: The Columbian Exchange transferred crops, animals, people, and diseases between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres, with catastrophic demographic effects on Indigenous Americans.
An estimated 12+ million enslaved Africans were transported across the Atlantic in the Middle Passage as part of the triangular trade system.
Spanish silver from Potosí, moved via the Manila Galleon trade, connected the Americas directly to Ming/Qing China's economy for the first time.
Labor systems (encomienda, mita, chattel slavery, indentured servitude) varied by colonizer and region but all extracted forced labor to generate colonial wealth.
traps: The 'discovery' of the Americas by Columbus is more accurately framed as sustained contact between two hemispheres that had been separate — millions of Indigenous people already lived there.
Disease, not superior European weaponry alone, was the primary cause of Indigenous population collapse in the Americas.
The Atlantic slave trade differed from earlier African slavery systems in that it was racialized, hereditary, and permanent (chattel slavery), not simply captivity from warfare.
Mercantilism, not free trade, governed colonial economic policy in this era — colonies existed to benefit the mother country's balance of trade, not to develop independently.

units.name: Revolutions 1750-1900

concepts.intro: Enlightenment philosophers challenged divine-right monarchy with reason, natural rights, and social-contract theory, and their ideas directly inspired the first successful colonial independence movement.
b: John Locke argued government exists to protect natural rights (life, liberty, property) and derives authority from the consent of the governed
Jean-Jacques Rousseau's 'general will' and Montesquieu's separation of powers shaped constitutional thinking across the Atlantic world
American colonists protested 'taxation without representation' after the Stamp Act (1765) and Tea Act (1773), invoking natural rights language
The Declaration of Independence (1776), drafted by Thomas Jefferson, used Lockean ideas to justify separation from Britain
The U.S. Constitution (1787) created a federal republic with checks and balances, though it preserved slavery and excluded women and Native Americans from full citizenship
The American Revolution became a model (and financial strain on France) that helped spark later revolutions

concepts.intro: Financial crisis, Enlightenment ideas, and deep social inequality under the Old Regime combined to topple the French monarchy and produce a radical, then reactionary, revolution.
b: The Old Regime's three estates (clergy, nobility, commoners) left the Third Estate paying most taxes while lacking political power
Deficit spending (partly from aiding the American Revolution) and poor harvests pushed Louis XVI to call the Estates-General in 1789
The Third Estate formed the National Assembly and stormed the Bastille (July 14, 1789), issuing the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

The Reign of Terror (1793-1794) under Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety executed thousands, including Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, to defend the revolution from internal and external enemies
Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in 1799, later crowning himself emperor (1804) and codifying legal equality for men in the Napoleonic Code while curbing political liberty
The Congress of Vienna (1814-1815) restored conservative monarchies after Napoleon's defeat but could not erase revolutionary nationalism and liberalism

concepts.intro: Enslaved and free people of color in France's wealthiest colony, Saint-Domingue, turned revolutionary ideals into the only successful large-scale slave revolt in history, founding the first Black republic.
b: Saint-Domingue's plantation economy relied on brutal sugar-plantation slavery, producing immense wealth for France on the backs of an enslaved majority
News of the French Declaration of the Rights of Man inspired free people of color and enslaved Africans to demand equality and freedom
Toussaint Louverture, a formerly enslaved general, unified rebel forces, defeated Spanish, British, and French armies, and abolished slavery on the island
Napoleon sent troops to restore slavery and French control; disease and fierce resistance under Jean-Jacques Dessalines defeated them
Haiti declared independence in 1804, becoming the first nation founded by a successful slave revolt and the second republic in the Americas
France and other powers diplomatically isolated Haiti and forced it to pay a crushing indemnity (1825) for 'lost property,' crippling its economy for over a century

concepts.intro: Creole elites, inspired by Enlightenment ideas and emboldened by Spain's and Portugal's weakness during the Napoleonic Wars, led independence movements across most of Latin America by the 1820s.
b: Creoles (American-born Europeans) resented peninsulares (Spanish-born officials) who monopolized top colonial offices under the casta system
Napoleon's 1808 invasion of Spain and Portugal removed the legitimate monarchs, creating a crisis of authority that colonial elites exploited
Simón Bolívar ('the Liberator') led independence campaigns across Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru, envisioning a unified Gran Colombia
José de San Martín liberated Argentina, Chile, and helped free Peru, coordinating a pincer strategy with Bolívar's forces
Miguel Hidalgo's 1810 Grito de Dolores began Mexico's independence struggle, which succeeded in 1821 under a more conservative creole-led coalition
Independence rarely improved conditions for Indigenous peoples, enslaved people, or the poor — creole elites simply replaced peninsulares atop existing racial and economic hierarchies

concepts.intro: Beginning in Britain around 1750-1800, a cluster of agricultural, technological, and economic changes shifted production from hand tools and human/animal power to machines and fossil fuels, reshaping the global economy.
b: Britain's advantages included abundant coal and iron, a stable banking/credit system, a large colonial market, and a labor supply freed by agricultural enclosure
The Agricultural Revolution (crop rotation, selective breeding, enclosure of common lands) raised food output and pushed rural workers into cities as wage laborers
James Watt's improved steam engine (1769) powered factories, mines, and eventually railroads and steamships, decoupling production from rivers and human muscle
The textile industry mechanized first: the spinning jenny, water frame, and power loom moved cloth production from cottage industry into centralized factories
Urbanization accelerated as factory towns like Manchester grew rapidly, often with overcrowding, pollution, and dangerous working conditions
Britain's head start let it dominate global manufacturing and trade through the 19th century, exporting factory-made goods and importing raw materials from colonies

concepts.l: Reactions & Consequences of the Age of Revolutions
concepts.intro: The political revolutions of 1750-1848 spread nationalism and liberalism across Europe and the Americas, while early industrialization generated new ideologies responding to its social costs.
b: Nationalism — the belief that people sharing language, culture, and history deserve their own sovereign state — spread from revolutionary France across Europe

Conservatives (favoring monarchy and tradition) and liberals (favoring constitutional government and individual rights) clashed throughout the early 19th century, notably in the failed Revolutions of 1848
Industrialization produced a new industrial working class (proletariat) facing long hours, child labor, and unsafe factories, sparking labor organizing
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels's Communist Manifesto (1848) argued industrial capitalism's class conflict between bourgeoisie and proletariat would end in revolution
Women's rights advocates, building on revolutionary rhetoric of equality, began organizing (e.g., Olympe de Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman, 1791; Seneca Falls Convention, 1848)
These revolutions collectively established Enlightenment-based political ideals — popular sovereignty, natural rights, nationalism — as enduring global forces even where they initially failed

keyFacts: The Haitian Revolution (1791-1804) was the only successful large-scale slave revolt in world history and produced the first Black-led republic.
Enlightenment natural-rights language (Locke, Rousseau) provided the ideological justification for the American, French, Haitian, and Latin American revolutions alike.
Latin American independence was led overwhelmingly by creole elites, not Indigenous or enslaved populations, and left existing racial/economic hierarchies largely intact.
Britain industrialized first because of coal/iron reserves, capital and credit markets, colonial markets and raw materials, and a labor force freed up by agricultural enclosure.
traps: Don't equate the American Revolution with a full social revolution — it changed political rule but left slavery and existing social hierarchies largely intact.
The French Revolution was not a single event: the moderate constitutional phase (1789-1792), the radical Terror (1793-1794), and Napoleon's authoritarian empire were distinct, shifting phases.
Latin American 'independence' from Spain and Portugal did not mean liberation for enslaved people or Indigenous peoples — creole elites largely replaced peninsulares at the top of the same system.

The Industrial Revolution did not happen everywhere at once — it began in Britain and spread unevenly to Belgium, the U.S., and Germany over decades, and most of the world remained agricultural into the 20th century.

units.name: Imperialism & Migration

concepts.intro: Industrialized nations built overseas empires from roughly 1850-1914 for a mix of economic, political, and ideological reasons, using technology that gave them decisive military and administrative advantages.
b: Economic motives included demand for raw materials (rubber, cotton, palm oil, minerals) and new markets for factory-made goods
Nationalist competition among European powers turned colonies into prestige symbols, fueling rivalries like the 'Scramble for Africa'
Social Darwinism and the 'civilizing mission' (mission civilisatrice) provided pseudo-scientific and religious justifications for domination, epitomized by Rudyard Kipling's 'White Man's Burden'
Technological advantages — the Maxim gun, steamships, quinine (to prevent malaria), and the telegraph — allowed small European forces to conquer and administer vast territories
Strategic motives included controlling naval coaling stations and canal routes (e.g., the Suez Canal, opened 1869) to protect trade and military reach

concepts.intro: European powers partitioned nearly the entire African continent in a few decades, formalizing their claims at the Berlin Conference without African representation.
b: The Berlin Conference (1884-1885) set rules for European powers to divide Africa, drawing borders with no regard for existing ethnic, linguistic, or political boundaries
King Leopold II of Belgium ran the Congo Free State as a personal possession, forcing rubber production through mutilation and mass violence that killed millions
Britain pursued a 'Cape to Cairo' vision under figures like Cecil Rhodes, while France expanded across West and North Africa
The Anglo-Boer (South African) War (1899-1902) saw Britain defeat Dutch-descended Boer settlers, using concentration camps that killed thousands of civilians
By 1914, only Ethiopia (which defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa, 1896) and Liberia remained independent of European colonial rule

concepts.intro: European powers, along with the United States and a rapidly modernizing Japan, extended formal and informal control over much of Asia through trade concessions, treaty ports, and outright colonization.
b: Britain ruled India directly after the 1857 Sepoy Rebellion (Indian Rebellion) ended East India Company rule, replacing it with the British Raj

China avoided full colonization but was carved into 'spheres of influence' after the Opium Wars (1839-1842, 1856-1860) forced unequal treaties (e.g., Treaty of Nanjing) opening treaty ports and ceding Hong Kong
The Meiji Restoration (1868) modernized Japan's military, industry, and government, allowing Japan to avoid colonization and instead become an imperial power itself (annexing Korea in 1910)
The United States acquired the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico after the Spanish-American War (1898), and fought the Philippine-American War against Filipino independence fighters
The Open Door Policy (1899), pushed by the U.S., sought equal trading access to China for all foreign powers rather than exclusive colonial control

concepts.l: Colonial Rule: Direct and Indirect Systems
concepts.intro: Imperial powers used varying administrative strategies to control colonized peoples, extract resources, and maintain order with minimal European personnel.
b: Direct rule (used by France) governed through European officials and aimed at assimilation, imposing French language, law, and culture
Indirect rule (used by Britain in much of Africa and India) governed through existing local leaders and institutions, which was cheaper but often entrenched or invented ethnic divisions
Cash-crop and extraction economies (cotton in Egypt and India, rubber in the Congo, sugar in the Caribbean) reoriented colonial economies to serve the metropole rather than local needs
Settler colonies (Kenya, Algeria, South Africa) saw large numbers of Europeans take land, displacing and often violently subjugating Indigenous populations
Missionaries spread Christianity and Western education alongside colonization, sometimes providing literacy and healthcare while also undermining Indigenous religions and cultures

concepts.intro: Imperial economies depended on massive movements of coerced and semi-coerced labor after the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade, reshaping the demographics of the Americas, Africa, and Asia.
b: Indentured servitude replaced much of the enslaved labor force after Britain abolished slavery (1833); Indian and Chinese laborers were sent under contract to Caribbean sugar plantations, South Africa, and Southeast Asian rubber/tin operations
Conditions for indentured workers were often brutal and closely resembled slavery, with long contracts, debt bondage, and high mortality
Forced labor systems like Congo's rubber quotas and French corvée labor compelled colonized Africans to work on infrastructure and cash-crop production under threat of violence
Chinese migration (the 'coolie trade') sent laborers to build railroads in the Americas (e.g., the U.S. transcontinental railroad) and work in mines under exploitative contracts
These migrations created lasting diaspora communities (South Asians in East Africa and the Caribbean, Chinese in Southeast Asia and the Americas) that reshaped colonial and postcolonial societies

concepts.intro: Colonized peoples resisted imperial rule through armed rebellion, cultural/religious revitalization movements, and early nationalist political organizing, with mixed success before 1900.
b: The Sepoy Rebellion (1857) in India began over religious grievances (greased cartridges) but grew into a broader revolt against East India Company rule, leading Britain to impose direct crown rule
The Boxer Rebellion (1899-1901) in China, led by anti-foreign 'Boxers,' targeted foreign missionaries and Christians but was crushed by an international coalition, deepening foreign control
Ethiopia's victory over Italy at the Battle of Adwa (1896) under Emperor Menelik II preserved its independence and stood as a powerful symbol of successful African resistance
The Zulu Kingdom under Cetshwayo won a notable early victory at Isandlwana (1879) against Britain before ultimately being defeated and absorbed into the British Empire

Early nationalist and reform movements — the Indian National Congress (founded 1885) and Chinese reformers like the Self-Strengthening Movement — began building political frameworks for later 20th-century independence struggles

keyFacts: By 1914, European powers controlled roughly 90% of Africa, a partition formalized at the 1884-1885 Berlin Conference without any African representation.
Japan's Meiji Restoration (1868) was the major non-Western exception: rapid modernization let Japan avoid colonization and become an imperial power itself.
Indentured servitude (especially of Indian and Chinese laborers) replaced much of the enslaved labor force after Britain's 1833 abolition, creating lasting diasporas worldwide.
Ethiopia's victory at the Battle of Adwa (1896) made it, along with Liberia, one of only two African states to remain independent through the imperial era.
traps: Don't call New Imperialism (c. 1850-1914) the same as earlier mercantile colonialism (1450-1750) — New Imperialism was driven by industrial capitalism, nationalism, and pseudo-scientific racism, and involved formal territorial annexation on a far larger scale.
Indirect rule was not 'gentler' than direct rule — it often deepened ethnic divisions (e.g., colonial favoritism in Rwanda) that had lasting, violent consequences after independence.
Indentured servitude was not the same as free wage labor — many indentured workers faced coercion, debt bondage, and conditions resembling slavery.

Resistance to imperialism was common, not rare — movements like the Sepoy Rebellion, Boxer Rebellion, and Adwa show colonized peoples consistently resisted, even though most rebellions before 1900 were ultimately suppressed.

units.name: Global Conflict 1900-present

concepts.intro: A tangle of long-term structural tensions and a single assassination combined to plunge Europe's great powers into a war of unprecedented scale by August 1914.
b: MAIN causes: Militarism (arms races, especially Anglo-German naval rivalry), Alliances (Triple Alliance vs. Triple Entente), Imperialism (colonial rivalries), and Nationalism (especially in the Balkans)
The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary by Serbian nationalist Gavrilo Princip (June 1914) triggered a diplomatic crisis
Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia activated a chain of alliance obligations, pulling Russia, Germany, France, and Britain into war within weeks
Trench warfare on the Western Front produced horrific stalemate and casualties, with new technologies (machine guns, poison gas, tanks, airplanes) making offense far deadlier than in prior wars
The war became 'total war,' mobilizing entire economies and civilian populations, including women who entered factories and support roles in unprecedented numbers

concepts.l: The End of WWI and Its Aftermath
concepts.intro: The war's end reshaped the map of Europe and the Middle East, while its punitive peace settlement and economic destruction sowed seeds for future conflict.
b: The Treaty of Versailles (1919) forced Germany to accept sole guilt for the war (War Guilt Clause), pay massive reparations, and lose territory and its overseas colonies

The collapse of the Ottoman, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, and German empires created new nations in Eastern Europe and the Middle East, often drawn without regard to ethnic realities (e.g., the Sykes-Picot Agreement dividing the Middle East)
The Russian Revolution (1917) toppled the Tsar and later brought the Bolsheviks under Lenin to power, taking Russia out of the war via the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk and founding the Soviet Union
Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points called for self-determination and a League of Nations, but the League lacked enforcement power and the U.S. never joined
War debts, reparations, and economic dislocation contributed to hyperinflation in Weimar Germany and set the stage for the Great Depression's global impact

concepts.intro: Economic crisis, humiliation from WWI, and fear of communism enabled totalitarian regimes to seize and consolidate absolute control over politics, economy, and society in Italy, Germany, and the Soviet Union.
b: Benito Mussolini's Fascist Party took power in Italy (1922), emphasizing extreme nationalism, a single-party state, and suppression of political opposition
Adolf Hitler's Nazi Party exploited the Great Depression, resentment over Versailles, and hyperinflation to win power legally in 1933, then dismantled German democracy
Totalitarian regimes used propaganda, secret police, and mass mobilization (youth organizations, rallies) to control both public and private life

Joseph Stalin's Soviet Union pursued forced collectivization of agriculture and rapid industrialization through Five-Year Plans, causing mass famine (notably the Ukrainian Holodomor, c. 1932-1933) and millions of deaths
Stalin's Great Purge (1936-1938) eliminated real and perceived political rivals through show trials, executions, and the Gulag labor camp system

concepts.l: Causes and Course of World War II
concepts.intro: Failed collective security, appeasement, and aggressive expansion by Axis powers in Europe and Asia led to the deadliest conflict in human history.
b: Germany's remilitarization of the Rhineland, annexation of Austria (Anschluss), and the Munich Agreement's appeasement over the Sudetenland emboldened Hitler's expansion

The Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact (1939) between Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union secretly divided Eastern Europe, and Germany's invasion of Poland (September 1939) triggered British and French declarations of war

In Asia, Japan's invasion of Manchuria (1931) and full-scale invasion of China (1937), including the Nanjing Massacre, expanded into a broader Pacific War after the attack on Pearl Harbor (December 1941)
Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union (Operation Barbarossa, 1941) opened a massive Eastern Front, ultimately draining German resources decisively at battles like Stalingrad (1942-1943)
The war ended in Europe with Germany's surrender (May 1945) and in the Pacific after the U.S. dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945)

concepts.intro: Nazi Germany's racial ideology culminated in the systematic genocide of six million Jews and millions of other victims, while atrocities occurred on multiple fronts of the war.
b: Nazi racial ideology targeted Jews as the primary victims, alongside Roma, disabled people, homosexuals, Slavic peoples, political dissidents, and Jehovah's Witnesses
Nuremberg Laws (1935) stripped German Jews of citizenship; Kristallnacht (1938) marked an escalation into open state-sponsored violence
The 'Final Solution,' formalized at the Wannsee Conference (1942), industrialized mass murder through death camps like Auschwitz-Birkenau, killing roughly six million Jews
Japan committed wartime atrocities including the Nanjing Massacre (1937-1938) and forced sexual slavery of 'comfort women' across occupied Asia
Postwar Nuremberg Trials and Tokyo Trials established precedents for prosecuting individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide

concepts.l: Global Consequences of the World Wars
concepts.intro: The two world wars devastated Europe and Asia, accelerated the decline of European colonial empires, and created new international institutions meant to prevent future catastrophic conflict.
b: The wars bankrupted European colonial powers, weakening their ability and legitimacy to maintain empires, which fueled decolonization after 1945
The United Nations (1945) replaced the failed League of Nations, aiming for collective security, with a Security Council giving veto power to major wartime allies
The United States and Soviet Union emerged as the two dominant superpowers, setting the stage for Cold War rivalry
Colonial troops from Africa, India, and other territories fought for imperial powers in both wars, and many returned home demanding independence in exchange for their service and sacrifice
The Holocaust's revelation fueled postwar Jewish demands for a homeland, contributing to the creation of the state of Israel (1948) and ongoing regional conflict

keyFacts: World War I's MAIN causes (Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism) turned a regional Balkan crisis into a continent-wide, then global, war.
The Treaty of Versailles's punitive terms (War Guilt Clause, reparations, territorial losses) fueled German resentment that Hitler and the Nazis later exploited.
The Holocaust systematically murdered approximately six million Jews, alongside millions of other targeted groups, through the Nazi 'Final Solution.'
Both world wars bankrupted and delegitimized European colonial empires, directly accelerating the decolonization movements of the mid-20th century.
traps: Don't treat WWI's assassination of Franz Ferdinand as the sole cause — it was a trigger, not the underlying cause; militarism, alliances, imperialism, and nationalism had built tension for decades.

Fascism (Italy, Germany) and communism (Soviet Union) are not the same ideology — both were totalitarian and used similar tools of control, but fascism emphasized ultranationalism and private property, while communism aimed to abolish class and private property.
Appeasement at Munich (1938) was intended to prevent war by conceding to Hitler's demands, but it is now widely seen as having emboldened further aggression rather than stopping it.

The Holocaust targeted multiple groups, not only Jews — Roma, disabled people, Slavic civilians, political prisoners, and others were also systematically persecuted and murdered, though Jews were the primary and most numerous target of the genocide.

units.name: Cold War & Decolonization

concepts.intro: The wartime alliance between the U.S. and USSR collapsed after 1945 into a decades-long ideological, political, and military rivalry that divided much of the world into competing blocs.
b: Ideological conflict pitted American capitalism and democracy against Soviet communism and one-party rule, with each side viewing the other's system as an existential threat
The 'Iron Curtain' (Churchill's term) divided Europe between Soviet-dominated Eastern Bloc states and Western democracies allied with the U.S.
The Truman Doctrine (1947) pledged U.S. support for nations resisting communist takeover, formalizing a policy of 'containment'
The Marshall Plan (1948) provided massive U.S. economic aid to rebuild Western Europe, partly to prevent communism from gaining appeal amid postwar devastation
NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955) formalized opposing military alliances, and Germany itself was divided into a communist East and capitalist West, symbolized by the Berlin Wall (built 1961)

concepts.intro: Direct U.S.-Soviet military conflict never occurred, but the superpowers fought for influence through proxy wars, arms races, and crises across the globe.
b: The Korean War (1950-1953) saw communist North Korea (backed by China and the USSR) fight U.S.-backed South Korea to a stalemate near the original border

The Vietnam War (U.S. involvement escalating through the 1960s, ending 1975) pitted communist North Vietnam against the U.S.-backed South, ending in communist victory and reunification under Ho Chi Minh's successors
The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) brought the world to the brink of nuclear war after the USSR placed missiles in Cuba, resolved through negotiation and mutual concessions
The Soviet-Afghan War (1979-1989) saw the USSR intervene to prop up a communist government, facing U.S.-backed mujahideen resistance in a costly, decade-long quagmire
The nuclear arms race produced the doctrine of 'mutually assured destruction' (MAD), a deterrent logic based on the certainty of mutual annihilation in any full-scale nuclear exchange

concepts.intro: Weakened European empires and rising nationalist movements led to rapid decolonization across Asia in the decades after WWII, though independence often came with partition and violence.
b: India gained independence from Britain in 1947 after decades of nonviolent resistance led by Mohandas Gandhi and the Indian National Congress under Jawaharlal Nehru

Partition (1947) split British India into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan, triggering mass migration and horrific communal violence that killed hundreds of thousands to over a million people
Vietnam's independence struggle against France (ending with French defeat at Dien Bien Phu, 1954) was followed by Cold War-driven division and the Vietnam War
Indonesia declared independence from the Netherlands in 1945, achieving full recognition after years of armed and diplomatic struggle by 1949
Ho Chi Minh and other Asian nationalist leaders often blended anti-colonial nationalism with communist ideology, linking decolonization to Cold War alignment

concepts.intro: Nearly all of Africa achieved independence between the late 1950s and mid-1970s, through both negotiated transitions and violent liberation struggles, often leaving fragile postcolonial states.
b: Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, became the first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence (1957), inspiring pan-Africanist movements across the continent
The Algerian War of Independence (1954-1962) against France was exceptionally brutal, involving guerrilla warfare, terrorism, and torture on both sides before Algeria won independence
The Mau Mau Uprising in Kenya (1952-1960) against British rule involved harsh British repression, including detention camps, before Kenyan independence in 1963
The Congo's rapid, poorly prepared transition to independence (1960) led to political chaos, the assassination of Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba, and Cold War intervention by both superpowers

Many postcolonial African states struggled with arbitrary colonial borders that grouped rival ethnic groups together, weak institutions, and continued economic dependence on former colonizers (neocolonialism)

concepts.l: The Non-Aligned Movement & Global South Solidarity
concepts.intro: Newly independent nations sought to avoid becoming pawns in the Cold War by forming a coalition committed to independence from both superpower blocs and mutual economic development.
b: The Bandung Conference (1955) in Indonesia brought together African and Asian leaders (including Nehru, Sukarno, Nasser, and Zhou Enlai) to promote decolonization, economic cooperation, and neutrality in the Cold War

The Non-Aligned Movement (formally founded 1961), led by figures like Josip Broz Tito (Yugoslavia), Jawaharlal Nehru (India), and Gamal Abdel Nasser (Egypt), rejected formal alignment with either the U.S. or USSR
Nasser's nationalization of the Suez Canal (1956) and the resulting Suez Crisis demonstrated growing Global South assertiveness against former colonial powers
Non-alignment did not mean isolation — many members still received aid or arms from both superpowers while formally avoiding alliance commitments
The movement highlighted shared Global South concerns: ending colonialism, promoting economic development, and resisting neocolonial economic dependency on former imperial powers

concepts.l: The End of the Cold War
concepts.intro: Economic stagnation, reform movements, and the collapse of Soviet political control over Eastern Europe brought the Cold War to a rapid and largely peaceful end between 1989 and 1991.
b: Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms — glasnost (openness) and perestroika (economic restructuring) — aimed to revitalize the stagnant Soviet system but instead accelerated its unraveling
Eastern European states threw off Soviet-backed communist governments in 1989 (the 'Revolutions of 1989'), symbolized by the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989
Germany reunified in 1990, and the Warsaw Pact dissolved as former Soviet satellite states pursued independent, often pro-Western paths
The Soviet Union itself dissolved in December 1991, splitting into Russia and fourteen other independent states, ending nearly 70 years of communist rule
The Cold War's end left the United States as the sole global superpower and prompted debates over a 'new world order,' globalization, and the spread of market economies and democratic governance

keyFacts: The Truman Doctrine (1947) and Marshall Plan (1948) established the U.S. policy of 'containment' aimed at stopping the spread of communism, especially in Europe.
India's 1947 partition into India and Pakistan triggered one of the largest and most violent mass migrations in history, killing hundreds of thousands.
The Non-Aligned Movement, formalized in 1961 out of the 1955 Bandung Conference, represented newly independent nations' attempt to avoid Cold War bloc alignment.
The Soviet Union's dissolution in December 1991 ended the Cold War, leaving the United States as the world's sole superpower.
traps: The Cold War was not a 'hot' direct war between the U.S. and USSR — the superpowers never fought each other directly, instead waging proxy wars (Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan) and an arms/space race.
Decolonization did not happen uniformly — some transitions were largely peaceful and negotiated (Ghana, India), while others involved prolonged, brutal violence (Algeria, Kenya, Congo).

Non-alignment did not mean total neutrality or isolation from the Cold War — many Non-Aligned Movement members still accepted aid or weapons from the U.S. or USSR while avoiding formal alliance commitments.

Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost and perestroika) were intended to save and strengthen the Soviet system, not deliberately dismantle it — their unintended consequence was accelerating the USSR's collapse.

quiz.q: Which West African ruler's 1324 hajj to Mecca was so lavish it reportedly disrupted gold values in Cairo?
quiz.e: Mansa Musa of Mali distributed so much gold during his 1324-25 hajj that it caused inflation in Cairo's gold markets.

quiz.q: The Song Dynasty's civil service examination system was based primarily on mastery of:
quiz.e: The examination system tested knowledge of the Confucian classics, reinforcing Confucian values in the bureaucracy.

quiz.q: Champa rice, adopted during the Song Dynasty, contributed most directly to:
o: A decline in trade with Southeast Asia
The collapse of the civil service exam
quiz.e: Champa rice matured quickly and resisted drought, enabling two harvests per year and supporting a population surge.

quiz.q: The Delhi Sultanate governed a population that was predominantly:
quiz.e: Muslim rulers governed a majority-Hindu population in South Asia, leading to a jizya tax on non-Muslims and cultural blending.

quiz.q: Zheng He's voyages are most notable for demonstrating:
o: Europe's early dominance of the Indian Ocean
Ming China's naval and diplomatic reach before turning inward
China's adoption of European navigation technology
The start of the Chinese civil war
quiz.e: Zheng He's fleets projected Ming power across the Indian Ocean world; the voyages ended when China chose isolationist policies.

quiz.q: Great Zimbabwe's wealth was based primarily on its role in trading:
quiz.e: Great Zimbabwe grew wealthy as an inland hub linking gold and ivory sources to Swahili Coast trading cities.

quiz.q: Swahili Coast city-states such as Kilwa developed a culture that blended:
quiz.e: The Swahili Coast fused indigenous Bantu culture and language with Islamic religion and Arabic trade influence.

quiz.q: In medieval European feudalism, a vassal typically received land (a fief) from a lord in exchange for:
quiz.e: Feudalism was a reciprocal system: lords granted land and protection, and vassals owed military service and loyalty.

quiz.q: The Great Schism of 1054 formally divided Christianity into which two branches?
quiz.e: The Great Schism split the Christian church into Roman Catholic (west) and Eastern Orthodox (Byzantine) branches.

quiz.q: The primary purpose of the Crusades (1095-1291) was to:
o: Recapture Jerusalem and the Holy Land for Christendom
quiz.e: The Crusades were religious military campaigns aimed at retaking Jerusalem and other holy sites from Muslim control.

quiz.q: The capital of the Mexica (Aztec) Empire, built on an island in Lake Texcoco, was:
quiz.e: Tenochtitlan, founded in 1325, became the magnificent capital of the Aztec Empire.

quiz.q: The Aztec Empire funded its capital and elite primarily through:
o: A tribute system imposed on conquered peoples
quiz.e: The Aztecs extracted tribute (goods, labor, sacrificial victims) from subjugated city-states rather than using money.

quiz.q: Aztec religious practice justified frequent warfare primarily because:
o: Captives were required for human sacrifice to sustain the gods
quiz.e: Aztec religion held that human sacrifice, especially to Huitzilopochtli, was necessary to keep the sun moving, motivating wars for captives.

quiz.q: The Inca Empire's mit'a system required subject communities to provide:
quiz.e: Instead of currency, the Inca state demanded rotational labor (mit'a) for roads, agriculture, and construction.

quiz.q: Inca administrators used quipu primarily for:
quiz.e: Quipu were knotted-cord devices used to record numerical and administrative information across the Inca Empire.

quiz.q: Compared to major Afro-Eurasian empires, the Aztec and Inca empires notably lacked:
o: The wheel, iron tools, and large draft animals
quiz.e: Despite complex political and engineering achievements, the Americas lacked wheeled transport, ironworking, and beasts of burden common in Afro-Eurasia.

quiz.q: The Abbasid Caliphate, centered in Baghdad, is best known for:
o: Preserving and expanding Greek, Persian, and Indian scholarship
Rejecting Arabic as a language of learning
quiz.e: Baghdad under the Abbasids became a major intellectual center, translating and building upon classical and foreign scholarly works.

quiz.q: Ibn Battuta is significant to historians of this era because he:
o: Traveled extensively through the Dar al-Islam and recorded detailed observations
quiz.e: Ibn Battuta's extensive travels and writings provide valuable primary source evidence about societies across the Islamic world.

quiz.q: Sufism contributed to the spread of Islam into West Africa and Southeast Asia primarily through:
o: Mystical, often syncretic missionary practices that adapted to local customs
quiz.e: Sufi mystics often blended Islamic practice with local traditions, making conversion more appealing and gradual.

quiz.q: The Byzantine Empire is best understood as a continuation of:
o: The Roman Empire in the Greek-speaking east
quiz.e: Byzantium preserved Roman law, administration, and Greek culture, blending it with Orthodox Christianity, after Rome's fall in the west.

quiz.q: A key similarity between the Mongol tribute system and the Aztec tribute system is that both:
o: Extracted wealth and labor from conquered populations without full integration
quiz.e: Both empires allowed local rule to continue in exchange for tribute payments, rather than direct annexation everywhere.

quiz.q: The Mandate of Heaven concept, relevant background for Chinese dynastic legitimacy, held that:
o: Rulers were chosen by popular vote
A just ruler had divine approval, which could be lost through misrule
quiz.e: The Mandate of Heaven justified dynastic rule as long as the emperor governed well; natural disasters or rebellion signaled its loss.

quiz.q: Timbuktu and Gao were significant West African cities primarily as centers of:
o: Trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt, and Islamic scholarship
quiz.e: These Mali Empire cities were vital hubs for trans-Saharan commerce and became renowned centers of Islamic learning.

quiz.q: Which best characterizes political organization in Western Europe circa 1200-1450 compared to Song China?
o: Europe was more centralized than China
Europe was decentralized under feudalism while China had a centralized bureaucracy
China had no bureaucracy at all
quiz.e: Feudal Europe distributed power among lords and monarchs with weak central authority, unlike China's centralized examination-based bureaucracy.

quiz.q: The Kingdom of Axum (Ethiopia) is notable in this period for remaining:
o: An isolated Christian kingdom amid surrounding Islamic states
quiz.e: Ethiopia preserved Christianity as a minority religious island surrounded by expanding Islamic influence in the region.

quiz.q: Griots served an important function in West African societies by:
o: Acting as oral historians preserving political and cultural traditions
quiz.e: In the absence of widespread written records, griots orally transmitted history, genealogies, and cultural knowledge.

quiz.q: The jizya was a tax that Islamic states typically levied on:
o: Non-Muslim subjects (dhimmi) in exchange for protection and religious freedom
quiz.e: The jizya was paid by non-Muslims under Islamic rule, granting them protected status and religious autonomy.

quiz.q: Which trade network most directly connected Mali's gold to markets in North Africa and the Mediterranean?
quiz.e: Camel caravans crossing the Sahara linked West African gold and salt to North African and Mediterranean markets.

quiz.q: The movable type printing developed under the Song Dynasty is significant because it:
o: Increased the speed and spread of written material within China
Replaced the need for the examination system
Led to the fall of the dynasty
quiz.e: Song-era printing innovations, alongside paper money and gunpowder, expanded the reach of texts and administrative documents.

quiz.q: The Yuan Dynasty differed from the preceding Song Dynasty chiefly because it was:
o: Founded by ethnic Han Chinese reformers
Established by Mongol conquerors under Kublai Khan
A return to pure Confucian rule
quiz.e: The Yuan Dynasty was founded after the Mongol conquest of China, with Kublai Khan employing foreigners like Marco Polo in his court.

quiz.q: The Ming Dynasty's founding in 1368 represented:
o: The restoration of ethnic Han Chinese rule and Confucian bureaucracy
The introduction of Islam as state religion
quiz.e: The Ming overthrew the Mongol Yuan Dynasty, reviving Confucian governance and the civil service examination.

quiz.q: Why did Ming China ultimately discontinue Zheng He's treasure fleet voyages?
o: The fleet was destroyed by Europeans
Court factions favored isolationist policies and reduced maritime spending
China lost a war with Japan
quiz.e: Confucian officials at court argued the voyages were costly and unnecessary, leading to a turn toward isolationism.

quiz.q: A defining feature of the Byzantine Empire's contribution to world history was its role in:
o: Preserving Greco-Roman texts and Orthodox Christian tradition
quiz.e: Byzantium safeguarded classical knowledge and Orthodox Christianity, later influencing the Renaissance and Slavic Orthodoxy.

quiz.q: Compared to the Delhi Sultanate, the Mali Empire's relationship with Islam was distinguished by:
o: Rulers embracing Islam while blending it with existing African traditions
No contact with the Islamic world
quiz.e: Mali's rulers, like Mansa Musa, adopted Islam and used it to connect with the wider Muslim world while local traditions persisted.

quiz.q: The primary reason historians compare state-building strategies across 1200-1450 empires is that most rulers relied on:
o: Similar tools — bureaucracy, religious legitimacy, military force, and tribute — despite different contexts
quiz.e: Despite cultural differences, states from China to Mali to the Aztecs used comparable methods to build and maintain power.

quiz.q: Which pairing correctly matches an empire with its record-keeping method absent full written script?
quiz.e: The Inca used the quipu, a system of knotted cords, to track numeric and administrative data without a full writing system.

quiz.q: The spread of Champa rice and improvements in agriculture during the Song Dynasty most directly led to:
o: Urbanization and population growth in China
The collapse of the imperial bureaucracy
quiz.e: Agricultural surplus from rice innovations supported larger cities and a growing population under the Song.

quiz.q: Cordoba in Islamic Spain (al-Andalus) is historically significant as a center where:
o: Only Muslims were permitted to study
Muslim, Jewish, and Christian scholars collaborated on translating classical texts
quiz.e: Al-Andalus fostered notable interfaith scholarly exchange, preserving and transmitting classical Greek and Roman knowledge to Europe.

quiz.q: The most accurate comparison between Aztec tribute and Inca mit'a systems is that:
o: Both extracted resources from subjects but through different means — goods/captives versus labor
Only the Aztecs taxed their subjects
Only the Inca had an empire
quiz.e: The Aztecs demanded tribute in goods and sacrificial captives, while the Inca required rotational labor service (mit'a) instead of goods or coin.

quiz.q: The Mongol conquest of Baghdad in 1258 marked the end of which caliphate?
quiz.e: The Mongols sacked Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid Caliphate's political power, though Islamic culture and scholarship endured elsewhere.

quiz.q: The Indian Ocean trade network relied heavily on which natural phenomenon for maritime navigation?
o: Trade winds blowing constantly in one direction
Monsoon winds that reverse direction seasonally
quiz.e: Sailors used predictable seasonal monsoon wind reversals to time voyages across the Indian Ocean in different directions.

quiz.q: Which network is most associated with camel caravans crossing arid desert terrain to move gold and salt?
quiz.e: The trans-Saharan network used camel caravans to move West African gold and Saharan salt across the desert.

quiz.q: The Pax Mongolica refers to:
o: A peace treaty between China and Europe
The relative stability across Mongol territories that facilitated increased Silk Road trade
The end of the Mongol Empire
quiz.e: Under unified Mongol control, trade routes became safer and more heavily traveled, a period called the Pax Mongolica.

quiz.q: The Black Death is believed to have spread to Europe primarily via:
o: Silk Road and Mongol-controlled trade routes from Central Asia
quiz.e: The plague traveled westward along overland and connected trade routes controlled or influenced by the Mongols.

quiz.q: A major demographic and economic effect of the Black Death in Europe was:
o: Massive population loss leading to labor shortages and higher wages for survivors
quiz.e: The plague killed roughly a third of Europe's population, creating labor shortages that increased the bargaining power of peasants and workers.

quiz.q: Which technology, invented in China, spread westward via trade routes and transformed warfare in the Islamic world and Europe?
quiz.e: Gunpowder, a Chinese invention, spread through trade and Mongol conquest, eventually revolutionizing military technology in Islamic states and Europe.

quiz.q: Buddhism spread from India into Central Asia and China primarily through:
o: Merchant and missionary activity along the Silk Roads
quiz.e: Buddhist monks and merchants traveling the Silk Roads carried the religion into new regions over centuries.

quiz.q: Islam's spread into West Africa in this era occurred mainly through:
o: Peaceful contact via trans-Saharan merchants and the conversion of ruling elites
quiz.e: Muslim traders crossing the Sahara introduced Islam, which West African rulers like those of Mali adopted, spreading it gradually.

quiz.q: Which port city served as a critical transshipment hub linking Indian Ocean and South China Sea trade?
quiz.e: Malacca's strategic location on the strait made it a vital hub for merchants moving goods between the Indian Ocean and East Asia.

quiz.q: Chinese junks and Indian/Arab dhows were significant because they:
o: Were smaller and less capable than European ships of the time
Were often larger and more advanced than contemporary European vessels
quiz.e: Asian shipbuilding, including Chinese junks and Arab dhows, was often more advanced than European shipbuilding in this period.

quiz.q: The four khanates that emerged from the division of the Mongol Empire included all of the following EXCEPT:
quiz.e: The Ottoman Empire was a separate Turkish state, not one of the four Mongol khanates (Golden Horde, Yuan, Ilkhanate, Chagatai).

quiz.q: The spread of papermaking technology followed a general path of:
o: China westward through the Islamic world to Europe
quiz.e: Papermaking originated in China and diffused westward via the Silk Roads and Islamic scholars before reaching Europe.

quiz.q: Gujarati merchants played a key role in which trade network?
quiz.e: Gujarati merchants from western India were prominent intermediaries in Indian Ocean commerce.

quiz.q: Timbuktu's importance in this era stemmed from its position as a center of:
quiz.e: Timbuktu grew wealthy and renowned as both a trading hub and a center of Islamic learning due to trans-Saharan trade routes.

quiz.q: The astrolabe, used for maritime navigation, was significantly refined by:
o: Islamic scholars building on Greek models
quiz.e: Islamic scientists improved upon earlier Greek astrolabe designs, aiding navigation across Indian Ocean and Mediterranean routes.

quiz.q: Which best explains why the Mongol conquests, despite their initial destructiveness, are seen as significant for trade?
o: Unified control over vast territory reduced banditry and tolls, boosting long-distance trade
They isolated China from the rest of Eurasia
quiz.e: Once established, Mongol rule provided a degree of order across Eurasia that made overland trade routes safer and more profitable.

quiz.q: Marco Polo's travels are historically significant chiefly because they:
o: Provided a widely-read European account of Mongol-era Asia, sparking European interest in eastern trade
Led to the fall of the Yuan Dynasty
quiz.e: Marco Polo's writings about his travels through Mongol territories and China fueled later European interest in Asian trade and exploration.

quiz.q: Hindu-Arabic numerals, which greatly simplified mathematics, spread to Europe largely via:
o: Direct trade with the Aztec Empire
Islamic scholars and trade contacts across the Mediterranean and Silk Roads
quiz.e: The numeral system, originating in India, was transmitted to Europe through Islamic mathematical texts and Mediterranean trade contact.

quiz.q: Which statement best compares religious spread along the Silk Roads versus the trans-Saharan routes?
o: Both spread religion exclusively through violent conquest
Both spread religion largely through merchant and missionary contact rather than conquest
Only the Silk Roads spread any religion
Only the trans-Saharan routes spread any religion
quiz.e: In both networks, religions (Buddhism on the Silk Roads, Islam on trans-Saharan routes) spread mainly through peaceful trade contact and gradual conversion.

quiz.q: The decline in agricultural labor supply after the Black Death most directly contributed to:
o: The strengthening of the manorial system
The weakening of feudal labor obligations and rising peasant wages in Europe
The founding of the Ming Dynasty
quiz.e: With fewer laborers available, surviving peasants gained leverage to demand better terms, undermining rigid feudal obligations.

quiz.q: Which of the following was NOT a major good traded across the Indian Ocean network?
quiz.e: Aztec cacao belonged to a separate, isolated Mesoamerican trade sphere, not the Indian Ocean network before 1492.

quiz.q: The camel saddle innovation was important to trans-Saharan trade because it:
o: Allowed camels to carry heavier loads efficiently across desert terrain
quiz.e: Improved camel saddles allowed merchants to load camels efficiently, making long, regular desert crossings commercially viable.

quiz.q: How did the Mongols generally treat the religions of conquered peoples?
o: They forced conversion to Mongol shamanism
They were generally tolerant, often allowing continued practice of local religions
quiz.e: Mongol rulers were pragmatically tolerant of diverse religions within their territories, aiding social stability across their empire.

quiz.q: A key difference between the Silk Roads and Indian Ocean trade network is that the Silk Roads were primarily:
o: Maritime while the Indian Ocean network was overland
Overland while the Indian Ocean network was maritime
quiz.e: The Silk Roads consisted of overland caravan routes, while the Indian Ocean network relied on maritime shipping powered by monsoon winds.

quiz.q: Swahili Coast cities functioned within the Indian Ocean trade network primarily as:
o: Intermediary ports linking African goods to Arabian, Indian, and Chinese markets
quiz.e: East African Swahili ports connected inland African resources like gold and ivory to the broader Indian Ocean trading world.

quiz.q: Which empire's taxation of trans-Saharan trade routes made it enormously wealthy, as demonstrated by its ruler's famous pilgrimage?
quiz.e: Mali taxed gold and salt trade passing through its territory, generating the wealth Mansa Musa displayed on his 1324 hajj.

quiz.q: The introduction of Champa rice and gunpowder into new regions illustrates the broader theme of:
o: Technological and agricultural diffusion via trade and conquest networks
quiz.e: Trade and conquest networks in this era enabled valuable technologies and crops to spread well beyond their origin points.

quiz.q: Compared to the trans-Saharan trade, the Silk Roads moved goods across a landscape best described as:
o: Arid steppe, desert, and mountainous terrain across Central Asia
quiz.e: Silk Road caravans crossed harsh Central Asian terrain including deserts, steppes, and mountain passes.

quiz.q: The devastation of the Black Death was most severe in regions connected by:
o: Highly interconnected trade routes linking Asia, the Middle East, and Europe
quiz.e: Areas most integrated into Eurasian trade networks experienced the fastest and most severe plague transmission.

quiz.q: Which best describes the religious composition encountered by trans-Saharan traders as Islam spread in West Africa?
o: Immediate uniform conversion of the entire population
A gradual, often elite-led conversion that blended with existing local religious practices
quiz.e: Islam spread gradually, often first among ruling and merchant classes, coexisting and blending with traditional African religious practices.

quiz.q: What role did diaspora merchant communities (such as Muslim traders in Indian Ocean ports) play in trade networks?
o: They served as trusted intermediaries who facilitated long-distance trade and cultural exchange
They had no lasting cultural impact
They only traded within their home regions
quiz.e: Diaspora merchant communities settled in foreign ports, building trust networks that eased trade and spread cultural and religious practices.

quiz.q: The Chagatai Khanate controlled which general region after the Mongol Empire's division?
quiz.e: The Chagatai Khanate ruled over Central Asian territories, one of the four successor states to the unified Mongol Empire.

quiz.q: Why is the period covered by Unit 2 often described as an era of the 'compression of time and space'?
o: Because expanded and intensified trade networks connected distant regions more quickly and reliably than before
quiz.e: Improved trade infrastructure and stability (like Pax Mongolica) allowed goods, people, and ideas to move across greater distances more efficiently.

quiz.q: The Ilkhanate, one of the four Mongol successor states, ruled primarily over:
quiz.e: The Ilkhanate governed Persia and much of the Middle East following the Mongol conquests, notably sacking Baghdad in 1258.

quiz.q: Which of the following best illustrates cross-cultural artistic diffusion facilitated by Silk Road trade?
o: Chinese silk and porcelain motifs influencing Islamic and later European decorative arts
quiz.e: Silk Road exchange carried not just goods but artistic styles and motifs, visible in Islamic ceramics and later European decorative arts.

quiz.q: The spread of the compass, originally developed in China, most directly benefited:
o: Maritime navigation and exploration across oceans
