quiz.e: A poorly prepared transition, combined with Cold War rivalry over Congo's mineral wealth, led to instability and Lumumba's assassination, partly involving foreign intelligence agencies.

quiz.q: A common long-term challenge facing postcolonial African states was:
o: Arbitrary colonial borders grouping rival ethnic groups together, weakening national cohesion
Complete ethnic homogeneity in every new nation
The total absence of any economic ties to Europe
quiz.e: Borders drawn during colonization for European convenience often ignored ethnic and political realities, fueling postcolonial conflict.

quiz.q: 'Neocolonialism' refers to:
o: Continued economic dependency and influence by former colonial powers over nominally independent states
The direct political re-annexation of former colonies
A movement for African political unity
quiz.e: Even after achieving formal political independence, many former colonies remained economically dependent on former colonizers through trade, debt, and investment relationships.

quiz.q: The Bandung Conference (1955) brought together which kind of leaders?
o: Newly independent and independence-seeking African and Asian leaders promoting decolonization and neutrality
quiz.e: Leaders like Nehru, Sukarno, Nasser, and Zhou Enlai met at Bandung to promote solidarity among decolonizing nations and resist Cold War bloc pressure.

quiz.q: The Non-Aligned Movement, formally founded in 1961, aimed to:
o: Avoid formal alignment with either the U.S. or Soviet Cold War bloc
Merge into a single Soviet-led state
quiz.e: Member states like Yugoslavia, India, and Egypt sought an independent path amid Cold War superpower pressure.

quiz.q: Gamal Abdel Nasser's nationalization of the Suez Canal (1956) led to:
o: The Suez Crisis, showcasing Global South assertiveness against former colonial powers
Immediate British and French annexation of Egypt
The permanent closure of the canal
quiz.e: Egypt's nationalization of the canal, followed by British, French, and Israeli military intervention, ultimately embarrassed the former colonial powers and boosted Nasser's stature.

quiz.q: Non-alignment during the Cold War did NOT mean:
o: Complete isolation from receiving aid or weapons from either superpower
Formal membership in either NATO or the Warsaw Pact
Rhetorical independence from Cold War blocs
quiz.e: Many Non-Aligned states pragmatically accepted assistance from the U.S. or USSR while avoiding formal alliance commitments to either bloc.

quiz.q: Mikhail Gorbachev's policy of 'glasnost' refers to:
o: Increased political openness and freedom of speech in the Soviet Union
A military buildup against the West
quiz.e: Glasnost allowed unprecedented public criticism of the Soviet government, exposing systemic problems and fueling reform pressure.

quiz.q: Gorbachev's 'perestroika' aimed to:
o: Restructure and revitalize the stagnant Soviet economy
Expand Soviet military presence in Latin America
End all economic activity in the USSR
quiz.e: Perestroika sought market-oriented reforms to fix chronic Soviet economic inefficiency, though it destabilized the existing system.

quiz.q: The 'Revolutions of 1989' refer to:
o: The largely peaceful overthrow of Soviet-backed communist governments across Eastern Europe
A series of violent coups in Latin America
The founding of the Warsaw Pact
The start of the Korean War
quiz.e: Popular movements across Eastern Europe (Poland, Hungary, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, etc.) overthrew communist governments largely without major violence in 1989.

quiz.q: The fall of the Berlin Wall (November 1989) symbolized:
o: The imminent collapse of Soviet control over Eastern Europe and the Cold War's approaching end
The start of the Cold War
quiz.e: The wall's fall became the iconic symbol of communism's collapse in Eastern Europe, foreshadowing German reunification in 1990 and the USSR's dissolution in 1991.

quiz.q: The Soviet Union formally dissolved in:
quiz.e: The USSR split into Russia and fourteen other independent states in December 1991, formally ending the Cold War and nearly seventy years of Soviet communist rule.

quiz.q: After the Cold War ended, the United States was often described as:
o: One of many equally powerful nations with no dominant power
Absorbed into the former Soviet Union
quiz.e: With the USSR's collapse, the U.S. emerged as the dominant global military and economic power in the 1990s.

quiz.q: Which best explains why decolonization accelerated rapidly after World War II?
o: European powers were economically and militarily weakened, and colonial nationalist movements gained strength and legitimacy
European colonial powers grew stronger after WWII
The United Nations forcibly ended all colonial rule immediately in 1945
Colonized peoples had no interest in independence
quiz.e: The war bankrupted and delegitimized European empires while colonial troops and nationalist leaders pressed harder for self-rule.

quiz.q: The doctrine of containment shaped U.S. involvement in which two major Cold War conflicts?
o: World War I and World War II
quiz.e: Both the Korean and Vietnam Wars stemmed from U.S. efforts to prevent the spread of communism as outlined in containment policy.

quiz.q: Why is the Cold War often described using the metaphor of a 'chess game' fought through proxies?
o: The superpowers avoided direct conflict, instead competing for influence through allied states, arms races, and regional conflicts
The two powers fought only using literal chess matches
There was no strategic competition at all
Both sides had identical political systems
quiz.e: Rather than fighting each other directly, the U.S. and USSR extended their rivalry into regional conflicts and competition for allies worldwide.

quiz.q: Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first prime minister, played a key leadership role in:
o: Founding the Non-Aligned Movement alongside leaders like Tito and Nasser
quiz.e: Nehru was a central architect of non-alignment, seeking to keep newly independent India free of Cold War bloc entanglement.

quiz.q: How did Cold War superpower rivalry affect African decolonization, as seen in the Congo crisis?
o: Both the U.S. and USSR intervened covertly to influence Congo's political outcome, worsening instability
Neither superpower had any interest in Africa
The Congo crisis was resolved without any foreign involvement
The UN prevented any foreign intervention successfully
quiz.e: Cold War competition for influence over resource-rich Congo contributed to the instability and violence following its independence, including involvement in Lumumba's assassination.

quiz.q: The Berlin Wall (built 1961) physically divided:
o: Communist East Berlin from democratic West Berlin
quiz.e: The wall became the most visible symbol of Cold War division, separating Soviet-controlled East Berlin from the West until its fall in 1989.

quiz.q: Indonesia's path to independence from the Netherlands involved:
o: A 1945 declaration of independence followed by years of armed and diplomatic struggle before full recognition in 1949
Immediate peaceful transfer of power in 1945
No resistance from the Dutch at all
Continued Dutch colonial rule through the 1960s
quiz.e: Sukarno declared Indonesian independence in 1945, but the Netherlands only fully recognized it in 1949 after years of conflict and negotiation.

quiz.q: Josip Broz Tito, leader of Yugoslavia, is significant in Cold War history for:
o: Leading a communist state that remained independent of Soviet control and helped found the Non-Aligned Movement
Ruling a fascist regime allied with Nazi Germany
quiz.e: Tito broke with Stalin in 1948 and steered Yugoslavia toward independent communism and later non-alignment.

quiz.q: Zhou Enlai's presence at the Bandung Conference (1955) reflected:
o: China's interest in building solidarity with newly independent Asian and African nations
China's alliance with the United States
China's rejection of any international cooperation
quiz.e: As a major communist power with anti-colonial credentials, China sought influence among the emerging Non-Aligned bloc.

quiz.q: What best explains the arms race between the U.S. and USSR during the Cold War?
o: Both superpowers rapidly expanded nuclear arsenals to deter the other from attacking, based on the logic of mutually assured destruction
Both countries agreed early on to disarm completely
Only the United States built nuclear weapons
The arms race ended immediately after 1945
quiz.e: Fear of falling behind militarily drove both superpowers to build ever-larger nuclear arsenals throughout the Cold War.

flashcards.d: Mali Empire ruler (r. 1312-1337) whose 1324 hajj to Mecca, distributing vast gold along the way, revealed West Africa's wealth to the wider Islamic and European world.
Ming Chinese admiral who led seven treasure fleet voyages (1405-1433) across the Indian Ocean to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and East Africa, projecting Chinese naval power and collecting tribute.
The 'House of Islam' — the interconnected Islamic world spanning Iberia to Southeast Asia, unified by shared faith, Arabic language of scholarship, and trade networks despite political fragmentation.
Islamic sultanate (1206-1526) ruling much of South Asia, imposing the jizya tax on non-Muslims and blending Persian-Islamic administration with existing Hindu culture.
Fast-ripening, drought-resistant rice variety from Vietnam adopted in Song China, enabling double-cropping and a major population boom.
Stone-walled trading kingdom in southeastern Africa (c. 1100-1450) that grew wealthy from gold and ivory trade linking the interior to Swahili Coast port cities.
East African trading cities (Kilwa, Mombasa, Mogadishu) blending Bantu and Islamic culture, trading gold, ivory, and enslaved people with Indian Ocean merchants.
Medieval European political-economic system organizing society through reciprocal land-for-loyalty and labor obligations among lords, vassals, and serfs.
Capital of the Mexica (Aztec) Empire, founded 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco, built on tribute extracted from conquered peoples across central Mexico.
Inca labor-tax system requiring subject communities to provide rotational labor for state projects (roads, farming, mining) instead of paying in currency or goods.
The 'Mongol Peace' — the period of relative stability and safety across Mongol-controlled Eurasia that allowed increased trade and travel along the Silk Roads.
Seasonal wind patterns that reverse direction predictably, enabling Indian Ocean sailors to time voyages between Africa, Arabia, India, and Southeast Asia.
Roadside inns along the Silk Roads that provided lodging, food, and security for merchants and their pack animals on long overland journeys.
Key Southeast Asian port city and Indian Ocean trade hub connecting Chinese, Indian, and Southeast Asian merchants; became an Islamic sultanate.

Bubonic plague pandemic that spread along Silk Road and Mongol trade routes in the 1340s, killing roughly a third of Europe's population and causing severe demographic and economic disruption across Afro-Eurasia.
Founder and unifier of the Mongol Empire, whose conquests created the largest contiguous land empire in history and enabled the Pax Mongolica trade era.
Traditional Arab/Indian sailing vessel with triangular lateen sails, used extensively in Indian Ocean trade.
Camel caravan routes across the Sahara Desert linking West African gold-producing regions with North African salt and Mediterranean markets.
Navigational instrument, refined by Islamic scholars from Greek designs, used by sailors to determine latitude by measuring the angle of stars or the sun.
The Mongol khanate that ruled over Russia and parts of Eastern Europe, one of four khanates formed after the Mongol Empire's division.
Ottoman practice of conscripting Christian boys from the Balkans, converting them to Islam, and training them as elite Janissary soldiers or imperial administrators.
Ottoman method of organizing non-Muslim religious communities (Christians, Jews) into self-governing units that paid the jizya tax in exchange for autonomy.
Ottoman sultan (r. 1520-1566) who presided over the empire's territorial and cultural peak, expanding into the Balkans and codifying Ottoman law.
Safavid ruler (r. 1588-1629) who reformed the military, promoted trade, and made Isfahan a center of Persian art and architecture at the empire's height.
Mughal emperor (r. 1556-1605) known for policies of religious tolerance (Sulh-i-kul), abolishing the jizya on Hindus, and integrating Hindu elites into administration.
Mausoleum built by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, completed in 1653, exemplifying Mughal architectural achievement blending Persian and Indian styles.
Mughal emperor (r. 1658-1707) who reversed Akbar's tolerant policies, reinstating the jizya tax and enforcing stricter Islamic law, straining relations with Hindu subjects.
Historians' term for large land-based empires (Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal) that used cannon and firearm technology to centralize military and political power.
First Russian ruler to formally take the title Tsar; centralized Russian power and expanded territory while intensifying autocratic and often brutal rule.
Qing Dynasty emperor whose long reign (1661-1722) expanded and stabilized Manchu rule over China, doubling territory and strengthening centralized administration.
The transfer of plants, animals, diseases, people, and ideas between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres following Columbus's 1492 voyage, with transformative global effects.
Spanish colonial labor system granting colonists the right to Indigenous labor and tribute in exchange for supposed protection and Christian conversion.
The brutal transatlantic voyage transporting enslaved Africans to the Americas, marked by extreme overcrowding, disease, and high mortality rates.
The transatlantic trade network linking Europe (manufactured goods), West Africa (enslaved people), and the Americas (raw materials like sugar and tobacco).
Massive silver mining site in present-day Bolivia, worked by forced Indigenous (mita) labor, whose output fueled global silver trade including with China.
Spanish trade route connecting the Philippines to Mexico, carrying American silver to Asia in exchange for Chinese goods like silk and porcelain.
Dominant early modern European economic theory holding that colonies should enrich the mother country through raw material extraction and favorable trade balances.
A system of permanent, hereditary, race-based enslavement treating enslaved people as property, distinct from earlier, less rigid forms of bondage.
Spanish conquistador who conquered the Aztec Empire (1519-1521), aided by Indigenous allies, disease, and superior weaponry.
A business structure (e.g., Dutch and British East India Companies) that pooled investor capital to fund and profit from risky overseas trading ventures.

18th-century intellectual movement emphasizing reason, natural rights, and consent of the governed as the basis for legitimate government, laying the ideological groundwork for the Atlantic revolutions.
The idea (Locke, Rousseau) that governments derive their authority from an implicit agreement with the people, who can withdraw consent if the government violates their natural rights.
Document drafted primarily by Thomas Jefferson justifying the American colonies' break from Britain using Lockean natural-rights philosophy.
Uprising that overthrew the Bourbon monarchy and the Old Regime's estate system, issuing the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen and eventually radicalizing into the Reign of Terror.
1793-1794 period of the French Revolution under Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety marked by mass executions of perceived enemies of the revolution.
French general who seized power in 1799, crowned himself emperor in 1804, spread revolutionary legal reforms (Napoleonic Code) across Europe by conquest, and was finally defeated at Waterloo in 1815.
Successful slave revolt in French Saint-Domingue that abolished slavery and created Haiti, the first independent Black republic and the second republic in the Americas.
Formerly enslaved general who led and unified the Haitian Revolution's early military campaigns against French, Spanish, and British forces.
Venezuelan-born 'Liberator' who led independence movements across northern South America (Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru), envisioning a unified Gran Colombia.
Late-18th-century shift, beginning in Britain, from hand production and animal/water power to machine manufacturing powered by coal and steam, centered in factories.
Meeting of European powers that set rules for partitioning Africa, drawing colonial borders with no African input and little regard for existing ethnic boundaries.
Pseudo-scientific application of 'survival of the fittest' to human societies and races, used to justify imperial domination as natural and inevitable.
Personal colony of Belgium's King Leopold II (1885-1908) where forced rubber extraction and violent punishment killed millions of Congolese.
Indian uprising against the British East India Company that began among Indian soldiers (sepoys); its suppression led Britain to replace Company rule with direct crown rule (the Raj).
Japanese political and social transformation that rapidly modernized the military, economy, and government, enabling Japan to avoid colonization and become an imperial power.
Two 19th-century conflicts (1839-1842, 1856-1860) in which Britain forced China to accept unequal treaties, open treaty ports, and cede Hong Kong.
Contract labor system, often coercive, that sent Indian and Chinese workers to plantations and mines worldwide after the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade.
Decisive Ethiopian victory over Italy that preserved Ethiopian independence, one of the few successful African resistances to European colonization.
Anti-foreign, anti-Christian uprising in China crushed by an international coalition of foreign powers, further weakening Qing sovereignty.
Colonial administration method (used extensively by Britain) governing through existing local leaders and institutions rather than European officials.
Mnemonic for World War I's structural causes: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, and Nationalism, which turned a regional crisis into global war.
